Our message to Nvidia's board:

Do not fire Jensen Huang.

There is no clear replacement for Jensen Huang. We are confident that his departure would ultimately be a net negative for Nvidia, its shareholders, and the AI Revolution.

First, take a look at the data. History also suggests that removing a successful CEO will come with a significant cost.

A study of 187 forced CEO departures from S&P 1500 companies found that removing outperforming CEOs resulted in negative long-term stock returns. This case would be no different, in our view.

Jensen Huang is the definition of an outperforming CEO. Nvidia's board must not make a decision in the heat of the moment.

The board should take the time to conduct a thorough investigation and consult with shareholders, with a strong emphasis on the latter.

Quite literally, Nvidia's board should convene a special shareholder meeting and hold an advisory vote on this decision. This is the most consequential CEO controversy in world history. Shareholders deserve a say.

In addition, Nvidia's stock, $NVDA, is now down -35% in 26 trading days, nearly half of which is a result of the recent scandal.

We believe Jensen Huang's potential removal as CEO is now ~80% priced in.

Why take an action with massive downside potential when the market has already priced in much of that risk?

The downside of retaining Huang may be limited, while the potential upside is tremendous.

Lastly, history shows that retaining Jensen Huang could still lead to a favorable outcome. In 2019, Amazon retained Jeff Bezos as CEO after his extramarital affair became public, and the company's stock subsequently surged +108% by 2021.

Personal misconduct should not be ignored, but it must also be distinguished from corporate wrongdoing and weighed against the consequences of removing an executive who is instrumental to the company's success.

We believe Jensen Huang is an irreplaceable part of Nvidia and the AI Revolution more broadly.

Once the dust settles, firing Jensen Huang would prove to be a costly mistake.

It is time to pause and consult your shareholders.

Former Cisco M&A head Mike Volpi on why he’s more optimistic about AI than the dot-com era: the internet built communication, AI is building intelligence.

Guido Appenzeller: “Is there one other big difference from how it was back then, which is that everything is now much, much larger? Back then we were investing a small fraction of a percent in infrastructure for the internet. Today we’re investing 2% or so of our GDP in AI infrastructure.”

Mike: “It is much bigger, but in the 100,000 feet abstraction, what is it that is being built? Back then it was communication that was being built. Today we’re building intelligence. And the economic value of intelligence is probably higher than the economic value of communication.”

“I also think that, believe it or not, it’s been nearly 30 years, the markets are more efficient now, which is why so much more risk capital is willing to make its way into AI.”

“So net is, I’m actually more optimistic about this cycle, but I also believe that there will be some correction and some cleaning up of the industry structure.”

@appenz @mavolpi

US pension funds are heavily concentrated in technology stocks:

The technology sector accounts for 44% of total US pension fund equity allocation, according to a Bloomberg analysis of more than 70 pension funds.

This percentage has more than doubled since 2015.

Pension fund equity allocation to technology is now larger than that of the next 3 sectors combined.

By comparison, Financials represent 16%, followed by Healthcare at 12%, Industrials at 11%, and Consumer stocks at 10%.

To put this into perspective, the Consumer sector was these funds' largest allocation in 2014, at ~20%.

US pension funds are more exposed to technology stocks than ever.

Mike Volpi explains why older GPUs are holding their value:

"We thought this asset had a five-year life ... If you're in the business of financing an asset and that asset ends up having a longer useful life, then you're the beneficiary of that."

" In theory, at some point when you have sufficient Vera Rubins, it doesn't really make sense to run H100s anymore because it's just a worse way of converting electricity into dollars."

"The problem is right now that the demand is so high that even if the watt-to-dollar conversion is low, you're going to still use the asset."

"Ultimately the scarcity is in the manufacturing of the semiconductor itself... And so then scarcity persists, then the life of the asset continues to be long."

The Machine Learning market is seeing accelerating growth.

The global machine learning market is now projected to grow from ~$100 billion in 2025 to ~$684 billion by 2033.

This implies a CAGR of +27.2% from 2025 to 2033.

As AI evolves, the focus is shifting toward AI models that can continuously learn, retain knowledge, and adapt to new tasks.

This represents a fundamental shift from AI systems that rely primarily on knowledge acquired during training to systems capable of improving through experience.

As adoption accelerates, demand for machine learning software, hardware, and services is expected to increase substantially.

We are watching this market.
